newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists seek cabinet, ignore protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists seek cabinet, ignore protests.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists start efforts to form a new government on Wednesday, rejecting calls by President Petar Stoyanov for immediate elections to help pull the country from a deep economic crisis.
Nikolai Dobrev, the interior minister of the ex-communist Socialist party, has seven days to put together a government after receiving a mandate from Stoyanov.
Opposition parties and thousands of student protesters quickly vowed to intensify efforts to force the Socialists to give up office nearly two years early and to hold elections.

"We must fight them together -- the (opposition) Union of Democratic Forces, the students in the streets, and the trade unions with their general strike," UDF leader Ivan Kostov told a Sofia rally of some 25,000 people on Tuesday.

The UDF said it would suspend its boycott of the 240-seat parliament to try to stop Dobrev from winning approval for a government. The Socialists have an absolute majority but the UDF is hoping defections could stop Dobrev.
"We'll be at the parliament to prevent the cabinet of Nikolai Dobrev being passed," UDF deputy leader Alexander Boshkov told Reuters.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov had to give the mandate to the Socialists -- parliament's biggest party and the caretaker government since Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21.
Against the backdrop of wheeling-and-dealing, thousands of students thronged Sofia for a 23rd day on Tuesday, keeping up their colourful rallies which mock the ex-communist leaders.
The students plan a torchlight rally on Wednesday evening and a contest to choose Ms Protest and Mr Vagabond -- critics of their daily rallies have dubbed them "mere vagabonds".
Three trade union groups have called on workers to back the students and opposition parties with a general strike, but such calls in the past have received limited support.
Four army and police officers' associations appealed for calm, saying they opposed the use of force against unarmed civilians.
Festive demonstrations were held in towns and cities around Bulgaria on Tuesday despite freezing weather. Thousands of protesters chanted slogans and waved blue UDF flags.

In the Black Sea port of Varna, students donned diving masks and snorkels to suggest the Socialists were at the helm of a sinking ship. Protests were also held in Plovdiv, Stara Zagora, Gabrovo and the main Danube river port at Rousse.

So far the Socialists have been unmoved by the protests or threats of general strikes. They appear determined to buy time, with Bulgaria in crisis -- inflation was 50 percent in January alone -- and public opinion clearly against them.
In one concession, the Socialists said they would hold national elections this autumn, more than a year ahead of the next scheduled vote in December 1998.

But opposition parties and students have said that with the lev in a freefall and forecasts that annual inflation could top 3,600 percent this year, there was no time to spare in getting a broadly supported government in power.
